text: ition of etoposide or tioguanine to induction protocols of cytarabine and daunorubicin appears to be equally effective in younger adults and children,11,12 but in older patients an induction regimen which added tiogua- nine was found to be more effective than one with etopo- side.13 As in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (see above) there is a trend towards the use of more intensive induction regi- mens.6,12 Use of high-dose cytarabine compared with standard doses potentially improves survival in younger patients with favourable cytogenetics, but in the elderly neurotoxicity outweighs any benefit;8 a combination of cytarabine with fludarabine may be an alternative in these patients.5 The use of haematopoietic growth factors is con- troversial; some allow for their use as an optional adjunct to intensive chemotherapy,2 while others recommend against their routine use in AML.1 Once remission is induced, consolidation or postremis- sion therapy is essential in preventing relapse.1,6,8 Options include further chemotherapy, or allogeneic or autologous bone marrow transplantation (see Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation, p.1811).1,2,7 There is no consensus on the best postremission therapy.2,7 Some advocate the use of high-dose cytarabine in those with favourable or in- termediate risk; others are candidates for allogeneic stem cell transplantation.2,7 Patients who relapse or who fail to achieve complete re- mission will require salvage therapy. Standard salvage regimens can include high-dose cytarabine or fludarabine plus cytarabine.7 Allogeneic stem cell transplantation can also be used for salvage therapy or for those in second or subsequent remission.2,7 Investigational therapy is also an option.7 Gemtuzumab ozogamicin may be useful in elder- ly patients.1 Non-myeloablative chemotherapy with allo- geneic transplantation may be an alternative in older pa- tients.5,7,14 Low-dose maintenance chemotherapy (with cytarabine and tioguanine) may improve disease-free sur- vival but not overall survival,4 and prolonged maintenance therapy is generally considered unnecessary in patients with AML.1,6,12 Where debility or other medical condi- tions make standard or investigational therapy impossible in the elderly, palliative treatment with oral hydroxycar- bamide, is often given; low-dose cytarabine may also be of benefit.1,3,7 Good results have been reported with a combi- nation of idarubicin and etoposide in elderly patients.5 Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) is a subtype of AML accounting for 10% of AML cases in adults.
